title: Medical physics
competency: Explain how X-ray, CT, MRI, ultrasound and radiotherapy use physics.

keywords.def: The use of physics to diagnose and treat disease.
X-ray imaging with a rotating source and detectors that makes slice images.

en.text: Medical physics uses physics to diagnose and treat disease. X-rays make a shadow picture: bone (calcium) blocks X-rays and looks white, air-filled lungs look dark. A CT scanner rotates the X-ray source and detectors and a computer builds slice images. MRI aligns hydrogen nuclei in a strong magnet and reads the energy they give back. Ultrasound uses sound above 20 kHz. Radiotherapy aims radiation at a tumour from many directions.

screens.title: A broken arm
screens.ask: A doctor needs to see if an arm bone is broken. Which is the quickest choice?
screens.after:
Bone blocks X-rays much more than soft tissue does.
So bone looks white and a crack shows as a dark line.
A stethoscope and a thermometer cannot see bone.

screens.title: Medical physics
paras: Medical physics applies physics to diagnose and treat abnormal tissue.
Roentgen discovered X-rays in 1895; this started medical physics.

screens.title: X-ray and CT
paras: X-rays are absorbed differently by different tissues, making a shadow picture.
Bone (calcium) blocks X-rays and looks white; the air-filled lung looks dark.
A CT scan rotates the X-ray source and detectors round the patient. A computer builds many slice images.

screens.title: MRI
paras: The body is mostly water, so it has many hydrogen nuclei (protons). Each acts as a tiny magnet.
A strong magnet lines them up; a short radio pulse disturbs them.
As they line up again they give back energy. Different tissues give back different amounts: the computer makes an image.

screens.title: Sound and radiation
paras: A stethoscope carries body sounds to the doctor's ears (Laennec, 1816).
Ultrasound is sound above 20 kHz; medical scanners use 3.5–10 MHz.
Radiotherapy aims X-rays or gamma rays at a tumour. The direction keeps changing to spare healthy tissue.

screens.title: Reading an ultrasound image
screens.text: Tap each term. Brightness = how many echoes come back.
items: Black. Fluid sends back no echoes.
Dark grey. Few echoes come back.

screens.title: Ultrasound wavelength
screens.ask: Change the scanner frequency. Watch the wavelength in body tissue.
screens.note: Sound in soft tissue: v ≈ 1540 m/s. Higher f → shorter λ → finer detail.

screens.title: Key words
defs: The use of physics to diagnose and treat disease.
X-ray imaging with a rotating source and detectors that makes slice images.

screens.text: Reading an X-ray picture: on an X-ray, bone looks white because
screens.why:
Different tissues absorb X-rays by different amounts.
Bone contains calcium, which absorbs X-rays strongly.
Little radiation reaches the film behind bone, so it stays white.
Trap: bone does not give off light.
Answer: calcium in bone blocks X-rays.
screens.clue: What happens to X-rays in bone?

screens.text: How MRI works: MRI images come from
opts: hydrogen nuclei in a strong magnetic field
screens.ans: hydrogen nuclei in a strong magnetic field
screens.why:
The body is mostly water, so it has many hydrogen nuclei (protons).
A strong magnet lines the protons up.
A radio pulse disturbs them; they give energy back as they relax.
Different tissues give back different amounts: that makes the image.
MRI uses no X-rays.

screens.text: Ultrasound range: which frequency is used by medical ultrasound scanners?
screens.why:
Ultrasound is sound above 20 kHz.
Medical scanners use 3.5–10 MHz.
5 MHz is inside that range.
2 kHz, 15 Hz and 500 Hz are ordinary (or too low) sound.

screens.text: Reading an ultrasound image: a fluid-filled region looks
screens.why:
The image is made from echoes.
Fluid sends back no echoes.
No echoes means no brightness: the region is black.
This is called anechoic ("no echo").

screens.text: X-ray vs CT: a conventional X-ray and a CT scan differ because CT
opts: rotates the source and detectors and uses a computer
screens.ans: rotates the source and detectors and uses a computer
screens.why:
Both use X-rays.
A normal X-ray takes one shadow picture from one side.
CT rotates the source and detectors round the patient.
A computer combines many views into slice images.
Trap: CT still uses radiation.

screens.title: MRI: put the steps in order
items: Protons return and give off energy
screens.why:
1. A strong magnet lines up the protons.
2. A radio pulse knocks them out of line.
3. The protons relax back and give off energy.
4. A coil detects that energy.
5. A computer turns the signals into an image.
screens.text: How MRI works: put the steps of making an MRI image in order.
screens.worked: Strong magnet aligns the protons → A radio pulse disturbs them → Protons return and give off energy → A coil detects the energy → A computer makes the image.

items.text: Discussion question 1.5, MRI: what disturbs the lined-up protons?
items.why:
After the magnet lines them up, a coil sends a short pulse.
The pulse is a radio-frequency wave.
It tips the protons out of line.
Then they relax and give off energy for the image.

items.text: Radiotherapy: the beam direction is changed often in order to
items.why:
The beam always passes through the tumour.
By changing direction, it crosses different healthy tissue each time.
So the tumour gets the full dose.
Each part of healthy tissue gets only a small dose.
Answer: to spare healthy tissue.

test.text: History of medical physics: X-rays were discovered by
test.why:
Wilhelm Roentgen discovered X-rays in 1895.
This started medical physics.
Laennec invented the stethoscope (1816).

test.text: Key word: ultrasound is sound with frequency above
test.why:
Humans hear up to about 20 kHz.
Sound above 20 kHz is ultrasound.
Trap: 20 Hz is the lower limit of hearing.

test.text: Reading an ultrasound image: a hyperechoic region looks
test.why:
"Hyper" means many.
Many echoes come back from it.
Many echoes make a bright region.

test.text: Diagnose or treat: which is a therapeutic device?
test.why:
Therapeutic devices treat disease.
A radiotherapy machine destroys cancer cells.
A stethoscope, MRI scanner and thermometer only find out what is wrong (diagnostic).

test.text: Reading an X-ray picture: the air-filled lung looks
test.why:
Air absorbs almost no X-rays.
Most X-rays pass through and reach the film.
A strongly exposed film is dark.
So the lung looks dark; bone looks white.

notes.text: Figure 1.13 caption: the first famous X-ray (1895) is of Roentgen's wife's hand, not his own.
p.13: MRI protons are hydrogen nuclei, not "free hydrogen atoms"; the pulse is a radio-frequency pulse from a coil, not a current through the tissue.
p.14: CT text cites Figure 1.18 (should be 1.15) and says source and detectors rotate "in opposite direction" (they rotate together, on opposite sides).
p.15–16: "KHz" should be kHz; hyperechoic areas look bright (white), not light grey.
